title: Ecclesiastes 9:11–18
context: The Preacher sees that success does not always go to the swift, strong, or wise: time and chance happen to all, and people are caught suddenly like fish or birds. He then tells of a poor wise man who saved a besieged city by his wisdom, yet was forgotten. Wisdom is better than strength and weapons, but it is often despised, and one sinner can destroy much good.

verses.text: I returned and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favor to men of skill; but time and chance happen to them all.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher saw “that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong” Arminian readers see a warning against trusting in one's own abilities: “time and chance happen to them all.” Outcomes are not guaranteed by skill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “chance” describes events as they appear to people, not outside God's rule. They read it with 9:1, where the righteous are “in the hand of God” Both traditions agree that human ability does not secure outcomes.

verses.text: For man also doesn’t know his time. As the fish that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare, even so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falls suddenly on them.
verses.arminianNotes: “For man also doesn’t know his time.” Arminian readers see the image of fish in a net and birds in a snare as a call to readiness, since disaster or death can fall suddenly on anyone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “his time” points to the hour of calamity or death, unknown to the person but not to God. Compare Luke 12:20, “tonight your soul is required of you.” Both traditions treat this as a sober shared truth.

verses.text: I have also seen wisdom under the sun in this way, and it seemed great to me.
verses.arminianNotes: “I have also seen wisdom under the sun in this way.” Arminian readers see the Preacher introducing a story that will show both the great worth of wisdom and how easily people overlook it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Preacher calls this example of wisdom “great.” After the sobering verses on time and chance, he still affirms that wisdom has real value.

verses.text: There was a little city, and few men within it; and a great king came against it, besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was a little city, and few men within it.” Arminian readers note the sharp contrast: a small, weak city against “a great king” with great bulwarks. Human strength alone offers no hope of escape.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the story is told simply, without names or a known historical setting. Its point lies in the contrast between overwhelming power and a small, defenseless town.

verses.text: Now a poor wise man was found in it, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man.
verses.arminianNotes: “Now a poor wise man was found in it.” Arminian readers see wisdom accomplishing what strength could not, as the poor man delivers the city by his wisdom, yet “no man remembered” him afterward.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that the city's savior is forgotten once the danger passes. The deliverance was real, yet the wise man who brought it receives no lasting honor or reward.

verses.text: Then I said, “Wisdom is better than strength.” Nevertheless the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.
verses.arminianNotes: “Wisdom is better than strength.” Arminian readers see the Preacher affirming wisdom's superior value, even while admitting that “the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that wisdom's worth does not depend on public recognition. Its value is real even when people prefer the loud voice of status. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him who rules among fools.
verses.arminianNotes: “The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him who rules among fools.” Arminian readers see a call to listen for calm, sensible counsel rather than following the loudest voice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast between quiet words and a shouting ruler. True authority lies in wisdom, not volume or position. Both traditions see this as practical wisdom held in common.

verses.text: Wisdom is better than weapons of war; but one sinner destroys much good.
verses.arminianNotes: “Wisdom is better than weapons of war; but one sinner destroys much good.” Arminian readers see personal responsibility: one person's choices can undo the good that many have built.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how fragile the gains of wisdom are. They see in this verse the destructive reach of sin, where a single act of folly can ruin much. Both traditions read it as a sober warning.
